articles.title: Australia's data centre boom drives the biggest capex jump in years, near mining-boom highs
articles.desc: The surprise is large, but the market reaction is likely to stay muted because so much of the spending is imported equipment that does little for local output or wages. Investors are more likely to focus on what it says about capacity pressure and the RBA's December decision, where any lift in hike
articles.content: The surprise is large, but the market reaction is likely to stay muted because so much of the spending is imported equipment that does little for local output or wages. Investors are more likely to focus on what it says about capacity pressure and the RBA's December decision, where any lift in hike odds would support the Australian dollar and push up short-term yields. The industry mix matters for equities: the boom is concentrated in data centres and technology rather than mining, which favours data centre operators, construction and electrical contractors, and power suppliers over the resources sector that dominated past investment cycles. --- Australia's investment boom is back near mining-boom highs, but this time it's being built from server racks rather than iron ore mines. Summary: Private capex rose 12.2% in the September quarter, against a 4.4% forecast and a 3.6% fall in Q2, and was up 18.6% from a year earlier Equipment, plant and machinery spending rose 23.1% to a record, while buildings and structures rose 1.7% Investment in information media and telecommunications, which includes data centres, rose 86.7%, with equipment spending up 183.5% Non-mining capex rose 16.0% against 1.4% for mining, and Victoria led the states with a 31.0% rise Firms' fourth estimate of 2026-27 spending rose 11.8% to about A$224 billion, with equipment plans up 20.4% Heavy reliance on imports will limit the GDP boost, and the RBA meets again on December 7-8 Australian business investment surged far beyond expectations in the third quarter. Private capital spending jumped 12.2% from the previous quarter, almost three times the 4.4% rise economists had forecast, Australian Bureau of Statistics data showed on Thursday. The figures, released at 0030 GMT (1930 US Eastern on Wednesday), put total capex at about A$59.5 billion for the quarter in inflation-adjusted terms, 18.6% higher than a year earlier. That takes it close to the peak reached during the mining investment boom more than a decade ago. The jump came almost entirely from equipment. Spending on plant and machinery soared 23.1% in the quarter and 34.3% from a year earlier, reversing an 8.9% fall in the June quarter and lifting it to a record. Investment in buildings and structures rose a more modest 1.7%. The industry detail points clearly to data centres. Total investment in information media and telecommunications, the industry that includes data centres, rose 86.7% in the quarter, and its equipment spending nearly tripled, up 183.5%. Earlier this year the ABS attributed a 6.5% jump in March-quarter capex to data centre equipment such as server racks and processing gear, and the June-quarter fall was widely seen as payback. Mining investment rose just 1.4%, while non-mining capex climbed 16.0%. Victoria led the states with a 31.0% rise. Firms also plan to keep spending. Their fourth estimate of capital expenditure for the 2026-27 financial year came in at about A$224 billion, 11.8% above the previous estimate. Planned equipment spending was revised up 20.4% to about A$102 billion, far outpacing a 5.6% upgrade for buildings and structures. There is an important caveat. Much of that equipment is imported, so a large share of the spending flows offshore rather than adding to domestic output. The boost to Australia's GDP will therefore be considerably smaller than the headline suggests. The ABS also completed its annual seasonal review with this release, which caused minor revisions to the equipment series. For the Reserve Bank of Australia, the data still adds to the case that the economy is running hot. The RBA raised its cash rate to 4.85% on November 3, its highest since 2008 and its fifth hike of the year, in a split 6-3 vote. The board said inflation remains broad-based and likely to stay above 3% for longer than previously expected, but it dropped its explicit warning about further increases. The RBA's final meeting of the year concludes on December 8, with the decision due at 0330 GMT (2230 US Eastern on December 7). October inflation data and third-quarter GDP figures will carry more weight before then, but strong investment intentions make it harder for the board to argue that demand is cooling. The figures also stand out against a global backdrop of growing resistance to data centre projects, from Tokyo's suburbs to Australia's own Northern Territory. In Australia's biggest cities, at least, the money is still being spent. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.desc: LSU and the SEC return to federal court Wednesday as the conference seeks emergency relief that could pave the way for the Tigers’ expulsion.
articles.content: Judge sides with LSU in latest court battle, but SEC expulsion vote can proceed BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WAFB) - A federal judge ruled against the Southeastern Conference on Wednesday, Nov. 25, in its legal battle with LSU over the university’s potential expulsion from the conference. According to multiple online outlets, the judge denied the SEC’s request for a temporary restraining order that would have prevented LSU from taking legal action to interfere with a potential expulsion vote. The ruling still allows the SEC to move forward with its Thursday, Dec. 3, meeting to consider kicking LSU out of the conference. Some context: The SEC can still continue - and presumably plans to continue - with its scheduled meeting next Thursday to consider expelling LSU. But for now, it does not have the protection of a federal court ruling, opening the door for legal challenges from LSU. However, LSU and the state of Louisiana could challenge the conference’s decision in court if member schools vote to expel the Tigers. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill has already vowed to sue the SEC if that happens. Wednesday’s ruling does not guarantee LSU will remain in the SEC. David Ridpath is a sports expert at Ohio University. “I don’t think it’s going to happen,” Ridpath said. “And the reason why is I think that LSU, this is my opinion, but I think that LSU will ultimately offer something in return. So what could that be? That could be an apology.” Ridpath said that even if it did move forward, there would be problems for other schools. Any vote would require a two-thirds majority of member schools, which would be 11 votes. “You can posture and bluster,” Ridpath added. “But, when you actually have to put your name on something… every school in the SEC lives in a glass house. So you need to be maybe careful about doing something like this." In a statement released Wednesday, the SEC said it respects the judge’s decision and confirmed its Dec. 3 meeting to consider LSU’s membership would proceed as scheduled. The conference said LSU representatives assured the court the university would not interfere with the meeting. “The members of the Southeastern Conference continue to share the expectation of adherence to agreed-upon Conference standards, appropriate oversight by each campus to ensure athletics programs fulfill those standards, and agreed-upon accountability when the standards are not met,” the SEC said. Louisiana pushes back against SEC lawsuit filed a motion Tuesday, Nov. 24, seeking to dismiss the SEC’s lawsuit The lawsuit stems from LSU’s attempts to add football and basketball players who were previously under contract with NFL and NBA teams. LSU argues that the football players in question were never added to its roster and that basketball player RJ Luis Jr. was removed from its roster after appearing in one game. that the state would sue the SEC if its member schools vote to expel LSU. Murrill called the potential expulsion an “unfortunate overreaction” and described LSU’s membership in the conference as a “billion-dollar proposition.” Murrill argued that the SEC could instead address the eligibility dispute through its existing complaint and investigation process. “I would like to see us get back to, you know, a situation where cooler heads are in a room,” she said. announced Monday, Nov. 23, that its presidents and chancellors would meet Thursday, Dec. 3 , to consider LSU’s continued membership in the conference. “The lawsuit seeks to protect the Conference’s ability to govern itself and to enforce the rules and policies its member universities have voluntarily adopted,” the SEC said in a statement Monday. Under conference rules, at least 10 of the SEC’s 15 other member institutions would have to vote in favor of terminating LSU’s membership. articles.title: Build a Kalshi Trading Bot in Python: From Zero to Ubuntu VPS Deployment (2026)
articles.desc: Real API data, fixed-point order books, automated tests, and a Linux service you can operate from SSH. The first thing I want to know when someone shows me a trading bot repository is whether I can run it. Not whether it has a dashboard. Not how many strategies the README mentions. Can I clone it on
articles.content: Real API data, fixed-point order books, automated tests, and a Linux service you can operate from SSH. The first thing I want to know when someone shows me a trading bot repository is whether I can run it. Not whether it has a dashboard. Not how many strategies the README mentions. Can I clone it onto a clean machine, start the application, inspect its output, and understand what happens when something fails? That's what we're going to do here. We'll build around a small Python project that reads Kalshi's public API, discovers open markets, reconstructs an order book, and continuously prints structured market snapshots. Then we'll move it to an Ubuntu VPS, run it under systemd, inspect the logs, and cover the problems you're likely to encounter during setup. The project has no trading credentials, no order-submission method, and no live execution functionality. What you'll get by the end: A working Python 3.11+ environment on Windows, macOS, or Linux. A read-only Kalshi market scanner that uses actual public API endpoints. A correct YES/NO order-book calculation using fixed-point prices. Automated tests and a deterministic offline example. An Ubuntu VPS deployment with SSH, a dedicated service user, and systemd. Commands for logs, restarts, troubleshooting, and basic operational checks. The project uses the Python standard library. No third-party dependencies are required. Verification: I reran the offline example and all 10 automated tests on November 25, 2026; they passed locally. The API paths were checked against Kalshi's official documentation. I could not verify a live Kalshi API connection or run the deployment on a real VPS from this environment, so those steps are provided for readers to execute and verify themselves. 1. What We're Actually Building The architecture is straightforward: Kalshi REST API | GET /markets?status=open Select a ticker GET /markets/{ticker} Confirm market is open GET /markets/{ticker}/orderbook Validate price levels Calculate YES / NO BBO Emit JSON snapshots Terminal / VPS systemd journal BBO means best bid and offer. The program has three commands: Command Purpose offline Read a synthetic fixture without internet access list Find open Kalshi market tickers scan Read one market's order book and publish a snapshot It also supports continuous polling, bounded API retries, and graceful termination. This is the foundation for a more sophisticated market-data service. It isn't an executable trading strategy. 2. Which Kalshi API and Python SDK Should We Use? Kalshi currently documents this production Trade API endpoint: https://external-api.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2 Public market-data requests do not need authentication. Kalshi also has a separate demo API: https://external-api.demo.kalshi.co/trade-api/v2 For authenticated applications, Kalshi publishes two official Python SDK packages: pip install kalshi_python_sync or: pip install kalshi_python_async The older kalshi-python package is deprecated. For this first project, I'm not using either SDK. We're making public GET requests with urllib.request, which is included with Python. That reduces the number of moving parts and makes the request path easy to inspect. It also means the project doesn't need an API key or a Kalshi account. Official references: Kalshi Market Data Quick Start Official SDK Overview Production and Demo API Environments 3. Get the Source Code GitHub repository: [INSERT PUBLIC REPOSITORY URL BEFORE PUBLISHING] The accompanying project is structured like this: kalshi-python-vps-tutorial/ ├── kalshi_reader/ │ ├── __init__.py │ ├── __main__.py │ ├── client.py │ └── book.py ├── examples/ │ └── sample_orderbook.json ├── tests/ │ └── test_reader.py ├── deploy/ │ └── kalshi-reader.service ├── .env.example ├── .gitignore ├── requirements.txt ├── README.md └── LICENSE client.py handles public HTTP requests and retries. book.py validates the fixed-point order-book data and calculates quotes. __main__.py provides the command-line interface. The test suite is in tests/test_reader.py, and the service file is under deploy/. Download or clone the repository and open your terminal in the project root. 4. Install on Windows Install Python 3.11 or newer from python.org. Open PowerShell and check the installation: py --version Navigate into the project: cd path\to\kalshi-python-vps-tutorial Create a virtual environment: py -m venv .venv Now start the offline example: .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m kalshi_reader offline You don't have to activate the virtual environment. Calling its interpreter directly also avoids PowerShell script-execution-policy issues. Run the tests: .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest discover -s tests -v If everything is installed correctly, the tests should complete without failures. We'll look at the actual expected output shortly. 5. Install on macOS Install Python 3.11+ from python.org or your preferred trusted package manager. Open Terminal in the project directory. python3 --version python3 -m venv .venv ./.venv/bin/python -m kalshi_reader offline ./.venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests -v The source code is identical on macOS, Windows, and Linux. Only the path to the virtual-environment interpreter changes. 6. Install on Ubuntu or Linux On Ubuntu 24.04: sudo apt update sudo apt install -y python3 python3-venv Then inside the project directory: The project requires Python 3.11 or newer. If your Linux distribution has an older version, use its supported installation method rather than replacing the system Python. Check the expected output The offline command reads a synthetic order book. The important fields should look like this: The actual program also prints a UTC timestamp and a note identifying the data as synthetic. I verified this output locally. At this stage, you've established that Python can import the project, parse its fixture, and calculate the book correctly. You haven't contacted Kalshi yet. That's intentional. When debugging installations, I prefer proving the local environment works before introducing network failures. 7. Connect to Kalshi's Public API Now we can retrieve actual market data. The program's market-discovery command calls: GET /trade-api/v2/markets?status=open&limit=20 On macOS/Linux: ./.venv/bin/python -m kalshi_reader list --limit 20 On Windows: .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m kalshi_reader list --limit 20 The scanner prints market tickers, titles, and statuses as JSON lines. You can narrow discovery to a particular series: ./.venv/bin/python -m kalshi_reader list --series KXHIGHNY --limit 20 KXHIGHNY is a series used in Kalshi's documentation. If there are no currently open markets in that series, run the listing without the filter. Important: use a current ticker Don't copy a market ticker from a tutorial written months ago. Prediction-market contracts expire, close, and settle. Use the list output to identify an open market. Then run: ./.venv/bin/python -m kalshi_reader scan \ --ticker YOUR_OPEN_MARKET_TICKER \ --once Replace the placeholder with an actual ticker. The program reads market metadata, checks its status, and requests the order book. It doesn't submit an order. Keep the scanner running Once a single scan succeeds: --interval 30 That polls the selected market every 30 seconds. Stop it with Ctrl+C. The implementation enforces a minimum 10-second polling interval and includes bounded retries for rate limits and transient server failures. For demo public data, add: --env demo The production and demo environments have separate datasets. Don't assume the same ticker is available in both. Market discovery is paginated The example's list command retrieves only the first page. Kalshi's /markets API uses a cursor for additional pages. The correct production implementation must preserve the returned cursor, stop when it is empty, and deduplicate by ticker. Kalshi documents that an invalid cursor can be ignored, causing the first page to be returned again. A collector that blindly appends every response could duplicate markets or repeatedly process the same page. That's a useful next improvement if you want a full market catalog. Reference: Get Markets API. 8. Kalshi Order Books: The Detail You Need to Get Right Kalshi's order-book response contains bids on two sides. An abbreviated response looks like this: { "orderbook_fp": } Each level contains: [price_dollars, contract_quantity] The values are fixed-point strings. The arrays are ordered by ascending price, so the highest bid is the last entry. There are no separate ask arrays. In a binary market: YES ask = $1.00 - best NO bid NO ask = $1.00 - best YES bid Using the sample data: Best YES bid = $0.42 Best NO bid = $0.56 Implied YES ask = $1.00 - $0.56 = $0.44 YES spread = $0.44 - $0.42 = $0.02 The best NO bid has 17 contracts in this example, so the implied YES ask has 17 contracts at that level. The size doesn't disappear when you convert the quote. Why I use Decimal Don't assume every Kalshi price is restricted to whole cents. Kalshi documents fixed-point price and contract-size representations, including support for subpenny pricing and fractional contract quantities in applicable markets. Python's Decimal avoids introducing binary floating-point errors into the conversion. Here's the essential calculation: from decimal import Decimal ONE = Decimal("1") def best_quotes(book): yes = [ (Decimal(price), Decimal(quantity)) for price, quantity in book["yes_dollars"] ] no = [ for price, quantity in book["no_dollars"] if not yes or not no: return None yes_bid, yes_bid_size = max(yes) no_bid, yes_ask_size = max(no) yes_ask = ONE - no_bid spread = yes_ask - yes_bid return { "yes_bid": yes_bid, "yes_ask": yes_ask, "yes_bid_size": yes_bid_size, "yes_ask_size": yes_ask_size, "spread": spread, This snippet demonstrates the math; it deliberately omits input validation. The actual book.py implementation also rejects invalid numeric values, prices outside the allowed range, and nonpositive quantities. It identifies two cases that should not be trusted as normal quotes: INCOMPLETE_BOOK — one or both sides have no resting bids. CROSSED_OR_LOCKED — the reconstructed spread is nonpositive. Don't turn either condition into an executable signal. An unknown ticker can also return an empty order book, rather than a useful 404 response. That's why the scanner checks the market metadata first. Reference: Kalshi Orderbook Responses. 9. What the Automated Tests Actually Verify Run: The project has 10 unit tests covering: Correct implied YES ask calculation. Empty order-book handling. Crossed-book detection. Invalid fixed-point prices and quantities. Missing response arrays. HTTP 429 retry behavior. Market-close handling. GET-only HTTP requests. Ticker validation. Offline command output. I reran these tests locally on November 25, 2026. Result: Ran 10 tests OK That means the tested functions behaved as expected with the supplied fixtures and mocked network responses. It does not mean we've proven live API connectivity, real trading performance, or uptime on a VPS. Those require separate tests in their actual environments. 10. Deploy the Kalshi Python Bot on an Ubuntu VPS Let's move the scanner off the development machine. For this lightweight read-only program, an Ubuntu 24.04 VPS with approximately 1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, and outbound HTTPS access is a reasonable starting configuration. That is a planning recommendation, not a measured hardware benchmark. You don't need a GPU or an exposed web application port. Step 1: Connect using SSH Create an Ubuntu VPS with an SSH public key configured through your hosting provider. From your local terminal: ssh ubuntu@YOUR_SERVER_IP Replace the address and username with those supplied by your provider. Step 2: Update the server On the VPS: sudo apt upgrade -y sudo apt install -y \ python3 \ python3-venv \ git \ rsync \ ufw Verify Python: Allow SSH before activating the firewall: sudo ufw allow OpenSSH sudo ufw enable sudo ufw status If you use a custom SSH port, allow that port instead. Confirm you can connect using your SSH key from another terminal before changing password-authentication settings. Step 3: Copy the source to the VPS From your local computer, in the directory containing the extracted project: scp -r kalshi-python-vps-tutorial \ ubuntu@YOUR_SERVER_IP:~/kalshi-reader-src Back on the VPS, create a dedicated system user and group. sudo groupadd --system kalshi-reader sudo useradd --system \ --gid kalshi-reader \ --home-dir /opt/kalshi-reader \ --shell /usr/sbin/nologin \ kalshi-reader Create the application directories: sudo mkdir -p /opt/kalshi-reader sudo mkdir -p /etc/kalshi-reader Copy the files: sudo rsync -a \ --exclude .venv \ --exclude __pycache__ \ ~/kalshi-reader-src/ \ /opt/kalshi-reader/ Keep the application source owned by root: sudo chown -R root:root /opt/kalshi-reader Create its virtual environment: sudo python3 -m venv /opt/kalshi-reader/.venv Now verify the code on the server: cd /opt/kalshi-reader sudo .venv/bin/python -m kalshi_reader offline sudo .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests -v Don't proceed just because the files copied successfully. Check the output. Step 4: Configure the selected market Use an open ticker from the market-discovery command. Create the service environment file: sudo tee /etc/kalshi-reader/reader.env >/dev/null <<'CONFIG' KALSHI_ENV=production KALSHI_TICKER=YOUR_OPEN_MARKET_TICKER CONFIG Replace the placeholder. Restrict access: sudo chown root:root /etc/kalshi-reader/reader.env sudo chmod 600 /etc/kalshi-reader/reader.env The service configuration will load this file through systemd. There are no trading credentials to store because we're only using public endpoints. Step 5: Install the systemd service The repository already contains a service file: deploy/kalshi-reader.service Its important settings are: [Unit] Description=Casatrick Kalshi Public Market Reader Wants=network-online.target After=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple User=kalshi-reader Group=kalshi-reader WorkingDirectory=/opt/kalshi-reader EnvironmentFile=/etc/kalshi-reader/reader.env ExecStart=/opt/kalshi-reader/.venv/bin/python -m kalshi_reader scan --interval 30 Restart=on-failure RestartSec=15 TimeoutStopSec=20 NoNewPrivileges=true PrivateTmp=true ProtectHome=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectKernelTunables=true ProtectKernelModules=true ProtectControlGroups=true RestrictSUIDSGID=true LockPersonality=true UMask=0077 StandardOutput=journal StandardError=journal SyslogIdentifier=kalshi-reader [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Notice a few decisions here. The service runs as kalshi-reader, not root. The application source is treated as read-only. Restart=on-failure restarts the process if it exits unexpectedly. Logs go to the system journal, so we don't need to expose a dashboard or create a public HTTP endpoint. Install the included service: sudo cp \ /opt/kalshi-reader/deploy/kalshi-reader.service \ /etc/systemd/system/kalshi-reader.service sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now kalshi-reader Step 6: Verify the service Check whether it started: sudo systemctl status kalshi-reader --no-pager Inspect recent output: sudo journalctl -u kalshi-reader -n 50 --no-pager Follow logs continuously: sudo journalctl -u kalshi-reader -f Restart the service after changing its configuration: sudo systemctl restart kalshi-reader Stop it: sudo systemctl stop kalshi-reader Check whether it is enabled for system startup: sudo systemctl is-enabled kalshi-reader Step 7: Verify recovery behavior A service reporting active (running) is only one piece of information. You also want to check: Is it receiving recent market-data responses? Is the selected market still open? Are JSON snapshots appearing at the configured interval? Are rate-limit or connection errors being logged? Can the service restart and resume operation? For a basic operational check: sudo journalctl -u kalshi-reader -n 30 --no-pager For reboot recovery, perform a controlled restart of the VPS when it's safe to do so, reconnect, and inspect the service status and logs. Deployment verification is still required. The steps above have been reviewed against the project's configuration, but they haven't been executed on a real Ubuntu VPS as part of this article. 11. Troubleshooting Problems You're Likely to Hit Here are common failure cases and where I'd start investigating. Problem What to check python: command not found Python installation and interpreter name No module named kalshi_reader Current working directory Invalid ticker Use an open ticker returned by list MARKET_NOT_OPEN The selected contract may have closed or paused INCOMPLETE_BOOK The order book lacks one or both bid sides CROSSED_OR_LOCKED Reject the quote as a normal trading signal HTTP 429 Increase polling interval; inspect retry behavior Connection errors DNS, outbound HTTPS, TLS, or service availability systemd service fails User/group, paths, environment file and permissions Service running but no valid quotes Check JSON statuses, timestamps and market lifecycle For Linux, start with: sudo journalctl -u kalshi-reader -n 100 --no-pager For network connectivity, test the public endpoint separately: curl -i \ "https://external-api.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2/markets?status=open&limit=1" If this request fails, the problem may be connectivity or API access rather than your Python parser. If it works but the application fails, inspect the response shape and the application's error logs. What happens when a market closes? The scanner checks market status before requesting the order book. If the market is no longer open, it emits MARKET_NOT_OPEN. It does not automatically roll to the next market. That would require a separate contract-selection policy using series information and market metadata. For a research scanner, this limitation is acceptable if it's documented. For an unattended production strategy, it would need deliberate handling. 12. What I'd Change Before Calling This a Production Bot The example works with REST snapshots. Kalshi's public market-data responses can be cached, and a snapshot can be stale by the time your process receives it. If your strategy depends on current order-book depth, you need a properly synchronized WebSocket feed. Kalshi's WebSocket order-book channel sends snapshots followed by incremental deltas. It also has sequence numbers and documented recovery behavior. A correct implementation would need to: Subscribe to the appropriate market. Build the initial order book from a snapshot. Apply signed level changes in message sequence. Detect missing messages. Request a fresh snapshot or resubscribe when necessary. Stop using the book if its state is uncertain. For conflated updates, Kalshi documents an additional subtlety: exchange clocks can decrease between delta messages. A consumer that discards every delta with a lower clock can corrupt its local book. That's why a production WebSocket implementation should follow the feed's sequence and recovery rules rather than invent a simple monotonic-clock filter. Reference: Kalshi WebSocket Orderbook Updates. And if we add trading, the project becomes considerably larger. It will need authenticated requests, durable order records, duplicate-safe submission handling, position reconciliation, risk reservations, partial-fill handling, and restart recovery. A running Python process with a working API connection isn't enough to claim production readiness. 13. What I'd Build Next The next iteration of this project should be a WebSocket market-data service. I'd give it five specific goals: Maintain a normalized order book per market. Track snapshot age and message-sequence continuity. Rebuild state safely after disconnects. Persist useful observations for research. Expose health information without exposing credentials or trading controls. After that, a separate demo-only execution project could test authenticated order-state handling using Kalshi's mock-funds environment. The demo environment is useful for testing supported workflows, but its liquidity and price behavior may not resemble live markets. I wouldn't claim the application is ready to trade real money simply because a demo request succeeds. That needs a different level of validation. 14. Building Something More Complex? If you've followed this guide, you now have the foundations of a Kalshi market-data service. You can run Python locally, discover markets, inspect an order book, test the parser, and work through deploying it as a background service. But maybe your project needs more than that. Maybe you already have a strategy and need reliable execution. Maybe you're connecting Kalshi and Polymarket. Or maybe you have a bot running on a VPS, but its order handling, latency, or recovery behavior isn't good enough. That's the kind of engineering work I focus on. I work on custom prediction-market trading infrastructure: API integrations, execution engines, risk controls, strategy automation, and production deployment. If you need a custom Kalshi or Polymarket bot built or an existing system fixed, contact me. Include your platform, what you need built or fixed, your approximate development budget, and timeline. I'll review the requirements and let you know whether it's something I can help with. Updated November 25, 2026. The example is read-only and educational. Local tests passed; live API and VPS deployment remain to be independently verified. articles.title: How to install Claude Code plugins (marketplaces, scopes & fixes)
articles.desc: How to install Claude Code plugins Checked against the official docs: Oct 21, 2026 Claude Code plugins bundle skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers so you can add a whole workflow or integration in one step. This guide covers installing from Anthropic's official marketplace and from other reposit
articles.content: How to install Claude Code plugins Checked against the official docs: Oct 21, 2026 Claude Code plugins bundle skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers so you can add a whole workflow or integration in one step. This guide covers installing from Anthropic's official marketplace and from other repositories, choosing a scope, keeping plugins updated, checking what a plugin can do before you trust it, and fixing the errors people hit most. Quick answer Open a terminal in your project and start Claude Code with claude. Run /plugin to browse the Discover tab, or open one plugin's details directly with /plugin install @claude-plugins-official. Read what the plugin will install, then choose a scope: you (every project), everyone on this repository, or you in this repository only. Type / and look for the plugin's skills, which appear as a command like plugin-name:skill-name. /plugin only works inside a Claude Code terminal session. To install from a script or a plain shell, use claude plugin install instead (see below). What a plugin is (and when you need one) A plugin is a folder of components that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit: skills (SKILL.md instructions), agents (subagents Claude can delegate to), hooks (commands that run at points such as after every edit) and MCP or LSP servers. Plugins come from a marketplace, which is just a catalog: a repository with a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file listing plugins and where to fetch each one. You don't need a plugin for a single skill or a single MCP server. A skill saved in ~/.claude/skills/ already works in every project (see how to create an Agent Skill), and one MCP server is a single claude mcp add command (see the best MCP servers for Claude Code). Plugins are worth it when you want several pieces packaged together, with updates from the marketplace. Install from the official marketplace Claude Code adds Anthropic's official marketplace, claude-plugins-official, the first time you start an interactive terminal session. It lists plugins Anthropic maintains plus plugins from partners and other authors. This example installs commit-commands, which adds commands for committing, pushing and opening pull requests: Inside a Claude Code session /plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official The command opens the plugin's details instead of installing straight away. Check Will install: the commands, agents, skills, hooks and MCP and LSP servers the plugin adds. For plugins in the official marketplace, a Context cost estimate shows what it adds to every message and what its skills add once loaded. Pick a scope (next section). Claude Code installs the plugin and any plugins it depends on. If the summary says Plugin is now active., you're done. If it says Run /reload-plugins to apply., Claude Code runs that reload for you when the panel closes. Then type / and look for /commit-commands:commit. The Installed tab in /plugin and claude plugin list in your shell also list the plugin with its scope. Pick a scope User (Install for you): every project on this machine. Saved in ~/.claude/settings.json. Project (Install for all collaborators on this repository): saved in .claude/settings.json, which you commit. That turns the plugin on for teammates but doesn't download it for them, so each person runs claude plugin install @ --scope project once. Local (Install for you, in this repo only): saved in .claude/settings.local.json. If the same plugin is set at several scopes, local beats project and project beats user. Install from your shell, the desktop app or VS Code From a shell or setup script, without starting a session (user scope unless you pass --scope): claude plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official claude plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official --scope project On a machine where nobody has opened an interactive Claude Code session yet, the official marketplace isn't registered, so add it first with claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official. Shell installs load the next time you start Claude Code, or after /reload-plugins in an open session. Desktop app (local or SSH session in the Code tab): click + next to the prompt box, choose Add plugins, select the plugin and a scope. VS Code extension: type /plugins to open Manage plugins and click Install on the Plugins tab. If the list is empty, add anthropics/claude-plugins-official on the Marketplaces tab first. Cloud sessions (including claude.ai/code) have no plugin browser and don't load the plugins installed on your machine. The terminal, the desktop app's local sessions and the VS Code extension share the same settings files, so a user-scope plugin installed in one shows up in the other two. Install from other marketplaces Many plugins live in their authors' own marketplaces, usually a GitHub repository. Add the marketplace once, then install by plugin@marketplace-name: /plugin marketplace add / /plugin install @ Claude Code prints the marketplace name when it adds it. Two real examples from our directory: Android Skills (Google) /plugin marketplace add android/skills /plugin install android-skills@android-skills Apify MCP Server + skills /plugin marketplace add apify/apify-claude-code-plugin /plugin install apify@apify The full Apify setup, including Cursor, Codex and the hosted server URL, is in how to set up the Apify MCP server. Anthropic also runs two other general marketplaces you add yourself: the community marketplace (/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community, install with @claude-community) and a small demo marketplace in anthropics/claude-code (named claude-code-plugins). Older tutorials often add the demo one; most of its plugins, such as code-review and commit-commands, are also in the official marketplace, so install them from there to avoid duplicates. /plugin marketplace add also accepts a full git URL, a local folder or an https:// URL to a marketplace.json. Recent versions can add and install in one step with --marketplace, for example /plugin install deploy-helper --marketplace your-org/plugins (Claude Code v2.1.275 or later in a session, v2.1.292 or later for claude plugin install). Plugins worth trying first This isn't a ranking and nobody paid to be listed. Each name below is in the official marketplace, so install it with /plugin install @claude-plugins-official. From Anthropic: commit-commands (commit, push, open a PR), code-review (multi-agent review of a pull request), feature-dev (a guided feature workflow with exploration, architecture and review agents) and security-guidance (security review of the code Claude writes). Code intelligence: language-server plugins such as typescript-lsp and pyright-lsp let Claude see type errors after its edits and navigate by symbol. Install the language server itself first; for TypeScript that's npm install -g typescript-language-server typescript. Services you already use: the official marketplace includes plugins named context7, github, playwright, sentry, supabase, linear, notion and figma. Our listings explain each tool: Context7, GitHub MCP Server, Playwright MCP, Sentry MCP, Supabase MCP. Skills: skill-creator helps you write, improve and test your own skills. Serena also appears in the official marketplace, but its maintainers ask users to install it with uv instead because marketplace entries can carry outdated commands. When a tool's own docs give a different install path, follow the tool's docs. Each enabled plugin adds the names and descriptions of its skills, agents and commands to Claude's context on every turn, and its MCP servers run alongside each session. Install the few you'll use. To see what an installed plugin costs, run claude plugin details and read the Always-on line; the Installed tab groups plugins you haven't used recently under Not used recently. Check a plugin before you trust it A plugin runs with your user permissions. Its hooks, MCP servers and language servers run outside Claude Code's sandbox, and its skills become instructions Claude follows. Anthropic's install screen says it plainly: Anthropic doesn't control what MCP servers, files or other software plugins include. Run claude plugin marketplace list to see where each marketplace came from. In the plugin's details pane, choose Open homepage or View on GitHub and read hooks/hooks.json (what each hook runs), .mcp.json (each server's command or URL) and anything in bin/. Prefer plugins from the company behind the service. Names such as claude-plugins-official are reserved: Claude Code only accepts them from github.com/anthropics/ repositories, so a third-party catalog can't pose as Anthropic's. Remember that updates can change what you reviewed. Auto-update is on by default for the official marketplace and off for third-party ones. Update, disable or remove plugins Run /plugin and press Tab to reach Installed. Select a plugin to disable, update or uninstall it, or press Space to toggle it. From your shell: claude plugin list claude plugin disable @ claude plugin enable @ claude plugin update @ claude plugin uninstall @ --scope project Updated plugins load in your next session, or after /reload-plugins. Removing a marketplace (claude plugin marketplace remove ) also uninstalls every plugin you installed from it. Common errors and fixes "zsh: no such file or directory: /plugin" You typed /plugin at the shell prompt. Run claude first and type it at the Claude Code prompt, or use claude plugin install @ in the shell. "/plugin isn't available in this environment" /plugin needs a terminal session. It doesn't run with claude -p, the Agent SDK, the desktop app's Code tab or claude.ai/code, and in the VS Code panel only /plugin or /plugins on its own opens Manage plugins. Use that surface's own install steps above, or a terminal. Marketplace "claude-plugins-official" not found The official marketplace isn't registered yet, which happens if you've only used the VS Code extension, a policy blocks it, or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_OFFICIAL_MARKETPLACE_AUTOINSTALL is set. Add it and retry: /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official The same fix applies when the Discover tab is empty or claude plugin marketplace list says No marketplaces configured. Plugin "" not found in any marketplace You left off @marketplace, so Claude Code only searched catalogs it already had. Name the marketplace (/plugin install @), which refreshes it first, or copy the exact name from the Discover tab. If the plugin lives in a third-party marketplace, add that marketplace first. "not found in marketplace" with a refresh hint Your local copy of the catalog is out of date. Refresh it, then install again: /plugin marketplace update Installed, but its skills don't show up Check Installed in /plugin (or claude plugin list) and make sure it's enabled. Open the Errors tab in /plugin; each entry says what failed. If you installed it during this session, run /reload-plugins. Open the plugin's details: a plugin that lists no skills has none to show when you type /. "This reload changes MCP tools â€¦ Run /reload-plugins --force to apply" Adding or removing a plugin's MCP server would invalidate the prompt cache, so Claude Code waits. Run /reload-plugins --force to apply it now (your next message re-reads the whole conversation), or start a new session. FAQ What's the difference between a plugin and an MCP server? An MCP server gives Claude tools. A plugin is a package that can include MCP servers along with skills, subagents and hooks. Many plugins in the official marketplace, such as github or sentry, package a service's MCP server for you. Do plugins work on claude.ai or in the desktop app? The desktop app's local and SSH sessions do (use + â†’ Add plugins). Cloud sessions, including claude.ai/code, don't load plugins from your machine. claude.ai and Cowork have their own plugin support with a different set of components. Using Cursor too? Cursor has its own plugin format and marketplace, installed from Customize. See Cursor Plugins, and how to add an MCP server to Cursor for single servers. Sources Commands and config above come from these official docs. Tools change often, so check them for the latest steps. Claude Code docs: Install and manage plugins Claude Code docs: Anthropic's marketplaces Claude Code docs: Plugins overview Claude Code docs: Plugin security and trust Claude Code docs: Troubleshoot plugins Claude Code docs: Plugin commands reference Claude Code docs: Code intelligence plugins anthropics/claude-plugins-official (marketplace.json and README) Android Skills README (plugin install) Apify docs: Install the Apify plugin in your AI agent Serena README (installation) Tools in this guide Claude Code Plugins (official marketplace) Claude Code Android Skills Apify MCP Server Serena Cursor Plugins (official) PluginStack is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by the companies mentioned. Spotted something out of date? Email pluginstackai@gmail.com. This guide was first published on PluginStack. Browse the PluginStack directory for more hand-checked MCP servers, plugins and setup guides.

articles.content: NASA spacecraft created stadium-sized crater after slamming into asteroid | United States NASA spacecraft created stadium-sized crater after slamming into asteroid The ESA's first detailed images of Dimorphos are here. This Hera Asteroid Framing Camera image shows Dimorphos in orbit around Didymos, with the crater caused by the 2022 DART impact clearly visible. The impact appears to have flattened one side of Dimorphos, leaving a crater that seems as wide as the impacted face of the asteroid and some weird structures inside it, including an apparent cigar-shaped structure at its center. After over four years of years of anticipation, the European Space Agency has obtained images detailing the aftermath of NASA’s head-on collision with the asteroid Dimorphos. The photos and scans from“Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same,” Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement. NATO and ESA Warn of Russian Nuclear Satellite Launch Threat “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once! ” Comparing images of the Didymos system before and after the 2022 impact of NASA’s DART mission with the smaller Dimorphos moonlet. The left-side image is a view from the DART spacecraft’s main DRACO camera shortly before impact. The right-side image is a view from Hera’s Asteroid Framing Camera, aiming to match the previous mission’s view angle as closely as possible. Credit: ESA Michel explained that while DART flattened one side of Dimorphos into a massive crater, the rest of the space rock isn’t much different. Fields of boulders largely remain where they could be seen in DART’s photos from 2022, although the event did drastically change the binary system’s surroundings. “Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size,” added mission scientist Michael Kueppers. Hera employed three instruments during its first observations—a thermal infrared imager to measure surface temperature, a 25-color multispectral imager, and a monochrome camera. The car-sized probe’s work is only just getting started, too. In December, Hera will ultimately travel to barely eight miles from the asteroids, while obtaining increasingly higher-resolution photos. The spacecraft will then deploy a pair of CubeSats to get even closer to the binary system in January 2027. If all goes as planned, one of those devices will even attempt to land on the surface of Dimorphos. The combined measurements from this phase will help researchers understand the impact’s efficiency and improve future deflection strategies. articles.title: FCC clears SpaceX to build up to 1 million AI data center satellites in space
articles.desc: The FCC approved the first U.S. constellation of orbital data centers and said it is reviewing other proposals
articles.content: FCC approved SpaceX plan for up to 1 million orbital AI data centers The FCC gave SpaceX approval for up to 1 million AI data centers in space The approval is granted in part with conditions, and SpaceX must file more orbital debris plans before deploying satellites above 600 km authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million satellites that would operate as data centers in space, according to an order the agency released on Wednesday. The FCC's Space Bureau granted SpaceX's application in part and deferred part of it, with conditions. The authority covers radio communications for the constellation, called Starmind, that serve as a fallback and in emergencies to carry telemetry and to track and command the satellites, in the 18.8-19.3 GHz and 28.6-29.1 GHz bands. SpaceX must operate in those bands on an unprotected, non-interference basis. The satellites will rely on optical links for their primary communications, the order said. The constellation would sit in orbital shells at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 kilometers (311 to 623 miles). The FCC deferred SpaceX's request for a waiver of the rule requiring satellites that end their missions below 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) to be disposed of through atmospheric re-entry. Before deploying any satellites that operate above 600 kilometers (373 miles), SpaceX must file an application to modify the authorization with a final orbital debris mitigation plan. The grant sets deployment milestones. SpaceX must deploy one satellite by Nov. 25, 2033, 10% of the authorized satellites by Nov. 25, 2035, and 50% by Nov. 25, 2038. It must launch the remainder by Nov. 25, 2040, or the authorization becomes null and void. The license term is 15 years and begins when SpaceX certifies that the first Starmind satellite is in orbit and operating under the authorization's terms. Three parties filed petitions to deny the application: Kuiper Systems, which operates as Leo; Viasat; and the American Astronomical Society. The bureau said it dismissed environmental and optical astronomy concerns as matters outside the Commission's authority. The proposal prompted a comment tally from the public north of 1,500, according to . FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the commission was, for the first time, approving orbital data centers. revealed the design of its first orbital data center satellite, called AI1 in June, ahead of its IPO. The orbital compute initiative was central to the company's pitch to investors. The FCC is weighing other proposals for data centers in orbit and plans to rule on every one, according to .
